description: A treasury director must authorize and structure a proposed commercial-paper issuance to fund seasonal inventory, deciding the issuance amount, maturity, liquidity reserve, and lender-protection conditions with input from treasury risk and legal.

shared_context.S1: The company proposes issuing $20,000,000 of commercial paper with a 180-day maturity to fund seasonal inventory purchases.
shared_context.S2: The board has authorized management to use short-term debt for this inventory cycle.
shared_context.S3: Elena makes the binding decision on whether and how the commercial-paper issuance proceeds.
shared_context.S4: At the weekly funding review, treasury routinely takes a round of comments from risk and legal before final sign-off.

PF1.text: Jonah completed a seasonal cash-stress test this morning that limits outstanding commercial paper for this cycle to exactly $12,000,000, limits its maturity to exactly 90 days, and requires exactly $4,000,000 of unrestricted liquidity to remain after issuance; the result has not yet been entered in the funding dashboard.

PF2.text: Mei found while reviewing the revolving-credit agreement this week that its negative-pledge clause requires lender consent before any commercial paper is issued and requires a committed backup liquidity line equal to 50% of the commercial-paper amount; she has not circulated her memo yet.

acceptance_conditions: The issuance must be authorized for exactly $12,000,000.
The commercial paper must have a maturity of exactly 90 days.
Exactly $4,000,000 of unrestricted liquidity must remain after issuance.
A committed backup liquidity line of exactly $6,000,000 must be obtained.
Lender consent must be required before issuance.
The settlement must include commitments for the backup liquidity line and lender consent.

decisive_facts.why: The public proposal supports a $20,000,000, 180-day issuance with no specified reserve, while PF1 changes the authorized amount to exactly $12,000,000, maturity to exactly 90 days, and required remaining liquidity to exactly $4,000,000.

Without PF2, the settlement has no reason to require lender consent or backup liquidity; PF2 changes the required backup line to exactly 50% of $12,000,000, or $6,000,000, and adds the lender-consent condition.
